abstract: Supply chain UI UX design plans the user experience (UX) and user interface (UI) of warehouse, transportation and planning software used on rugged handhelds, truck tablets and control-room screens. Our supply chain design sprints take 4–8 weeks, cost $25,000–$60,000, and include floor observation, glove-friendly scan flows and exception screens tested with operators.

sections.h2: What is supply chain UI UX design?
sections.answer: Supply chain UI UX design is the research, interaction design and visual design of software that receives, stores, picks, ships, plans and tracks goods. Users include pickers, forklift drivers, dispatchers and planners who work standing, moving, gloved and against time targets.
sections.body: A warehouse management system (WMS) screen is read at arm's length on a 4–6 inch handheld while the operator holds a carton, so the scan prompt, quantity and location code matter more than navigation. Planners at desks face thousands of stock keeping units (SKUs) and forecast exceptions on wide monitors. Control-tower views for dispatch teams follow our dashboard UX design method.

sections.h2: Which warehouse, transport and planning tools do we design?
sections.answer: We design 5 types of supply chain products: WMS mobile apps, transportation management software, planning tools, fleet and yard apps, and real-time operations dashboards.

items.title: WMS mobile apps.
items.body: Receiving, picking and cycle counts run on handheld scanners, for example a pick screen that shows bin location, item image and quantity in 3 lines.

items.title: Transportation management system (TMS) software.
items.body: Shippers tender loads and track shipments, for example a load board that flags tenders still waiting for carrier acceptance.

items.title: Planning and forecasting tools.
items.body: Planners override forecasts with a reason, for example an exception list ranking SKUs by forecast error and stockout risk.

items.title: Fleet and yard apps.
items.body: Drivers capture proof of delivery and yard staff move trailers, for example a yard map that colours each trailer by dwell time.

items.title: Real-time operations dashboards.
items.body: Supervisors watch throughput on wall displays, for example a dock view showing trucks waiting and orders at risk of missing carrier cut-off.

sections.h2: What UX challenges are specific to supply chain?
sections.answer: Supply chain UX faces 4 specific challenges: gloved one-handed use, poor light and noise, interrupted work and exceptions at volume.

items.title: Gloves, rugged devices and one-handed use
items.body: Operators wear gloves and hold cartons, so targets are 48 px or larger and key steps map to the hardware scan trigger.

items.title: Low light, glare and noise
items.body: Freezers, dock doors and night shifts change visibility, so screens use high-contrast themes, large numerals and vibration feedback instead of sounds.

items.title: Interrupted, task-switching work
items.body: Pickers stop for replenishment or a supervisor question, so every task saves state on each scan and resumes at the exact step after a device sleeps or drops Wi-Fi.

items.title: Exception handling at volume
items.body: Short picks, damaged goods and late carriers break the happy path, so exception flows offer predefined reason codes, photo capture and a named owner for each issue.

sections.h2: How does our supply chain UI UX design process work?
sections.answer: Our supply chain design process takes 4–8 weeks (20–40 working days) and runs in 4 steps, with at least 1 site visit.

items.title: Floor observation (3–5 days)
items.body: Researchers shadow pickers and dispatchers across shifts and record scan sequences and interruptions.

items.title: Workflow and exception mapping (3–6 days)
items.body: Each task is mapped scan by scan with exception branches, then checked against WMS or TMS business rules.

items.title: Device-specific interaction design (8–14 days)
items.body: Designers build handheld, tablet and desktop screens with glove-sized targets, scan-trigger mapping and offline states.

items.title: On-floor usability testing and handover (6–15 days)
items.body: Operators test the prototype on real devices, wearing their own gloves, in the aisles and docks, then developers receive annotated Figma files and device specs.

sections.h2: Warehouse floor UX vs office software UX
sections.answer: Supply chain UX serves physical work on rugged devices and measures throughput; general product UX serves seated screen use and measures growth.

sections.h2: How much does supply chain UI UX design cost?
sections.answer: A supply chain research and design sprint costs $25,000–$60,000 over 4–8 weeks. The price depends on 4 factors: the number of sites visited, the number of device types, the number of operator roles and the number of exception flows.
sections.body: A handheld picking app for 1 warehouse and 2 roles sits near $25,000. A WMS suite with picking, shipping, a supervisor dashboard and 2 site visits sits near $60,000. An existing scanner app with high training time starts with UX audit services at $5,000–$15,000.

sections.h2: Which safety and data standards shape supply chain UX?
sections.answer: 5 standards and regulations shape supply chain UX: OSHA forklift rules, FMCSA driver rules, GS1 barcodes, DSCSA and WCAG 2.2.
items: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) powered industrial truck standard (29 CFR 1910.178): forklift-mounted apps lock non-essential input while the truck moves.
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) rules (49 CFR 392.80 and 392.82): driver apps block texting and handheld interaction while the vehicle moves.
GS1 barcode standards: scan flows accept GS1-128, GS1 DataMatrix and Serial Shipping Container Code (SSCC) labels and display parsed lot, expiry and serial fields.
Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA): pharmaceutical warehouses verify product identifiers at receiving, so screens show serial-number checks and flag suspect product.
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 level AA: shipper and carrier portals meet 4.5:1 text contrast, and handheld targets exceed the 24×24 CSS pixel minimum.

sections.h2: Supply chain UI UX design FAQs
sections.answer: These answers cover 5 questions logistics software teams ask before an engagement.

faqs.q: Do you design for Zebra and Honeywell handheld scanners?
faqs.a: Yes. Designs target the screen size and scan trigger of the customer's devices, for example Zebra TC-series and Honeywell CT-series handhelds, and testing runs on the physical devices.

faqs.q: Can a WMS app work without Wi-Fi?
faqs.a: Yes. Offline-first designs queue scans on the device, show sync status on every screen and resolve conflicts on reconnection, for freezers, steel racking and yards with weak coverage.

faqs.q: Do warehouse designs need testing on the floor?
faqs.a: Yes. On-floor tests with gloves, real stock and normal noise expose problems a desk test misses, for example a quantity field too small to read at arm's length.

faqs.q: Is a desktop WMS screen enough for supervisors?
faqs.a: No. Supervisors walk the floor, so supervisor tools need a tablet view for labour assignment and exceptions, plus a wall-display dashboard for throughput and backlog.

faqs.q: How long does a supply chain design project take?
faqs.a: A supply chain research and design sprint takes 4–8 weeks, which equals 20–40 working days. A full WMS, TMS or planning platform with a design system takes 8–16 weeks.
